questions.question: How do you test reactive Spring code with StepVerifier and WebTestClient?
questions.title: Testing Reactive Code — StepVerifier, WebTestClient, BlockHound
questions.direct_answer: Reactive testing uses specialized tools because regular JUnit assertions don't wait for async signals. **`StepVerifier`** (from `reactor-test`) is the primary tool for verifying `Mono` / `Flux` sequences — chain expectations like `expectNext`, `expectError`, `thenRequest`, then call `.verify()`. **`WebTestClient`** is the reactive alternative to MockMvc — slice-level via `@WebFluxTest` or full-stack via `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)`. Use **MockWebServer** to fake `WebClient` upstreams, **Testcontainers** for real R2DBC / Kafka, and enable **BlockHound** to catch accidental blocking on event-loop threads. Always end `StepVerifier` chains with `.verify()` — without it the test passes trivially because nothing subscribed.

sections.title: The Reactive Testing Toolkit
sections.content:
Reactive code can't be tested with plain `assertEquals` because results come asynchronously. You need tools that subscribe, collect signals, and let you assert on them.

**Core tools you'll use:**
- **`StepVerifier`** (from `io.projectreactor:reactor-test`) — verifies `Mono` / `Flux` signals step by step; the workhorse for unit-testing reactive chains
- **`TestPublisher`** — creates controllable `Mono` / `Flux` for feeding custom sequences into code under test
- **`WebTestClient`** — end-to-end HTTP testing for WebFlux endpoints; either against a running server or in-memory mock mode
- **MockWebServer (okhttp)** — simulates upstream services for `WebClient` testing
- **`BlockHound`** — JVM agent that throws on blocking calls inside Reactor's non-blocking schedulers
- **Testcontainers** — real PostgreSQL / Mongo / Redis / Kafka in Docker for integration tests
- **Spring Boot test slices** — `@SpringBootTest`, `@DataR2dbcTest`, `@WebFluxTest`

**Test layers:**
- **Unit** — pure Reactor chains with `StepVerifier` and in-memory data
- **Slice** — `@WebFluxTest` for controllers with mocked services; `@DataR2dbcTest` for repositories
- **Integration** — `@SpringBootTest` plus `WebTestClient` plus Testcontainers

The single most important rule: every reactive test needs a subscriber. Without `.verify()` (`StepVerifier`) or `.exchange()` (`WebTestClient`) the chain never runs and the test passes trivially.

WebTestClient and Controller Slices

BlockHound, Debug Hooks, Pyramids, and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
**When BlockHound helps:**
- Detects blocking calls on Reactor's non-blocking schedulers (event loop, `parallel`)
- Catches accidental `Thread.sleep`, blocking JDBC, blocking file I/O on the wrong scheduler
- Should be enabled for every reactive test class

**When BlockHound hurts:**
- Throws on legitimate blocking inside `boundedElastic` if misconfigured
- Whitelist known-blocking legacy methods if necessary

```java
@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)
class BlockHoundSetup {
    @BeforeAll
    static void install() {
        BlockHound.install();
    }
}
```

Whitelist explicitly when needed:

```java
BlockHound.install(builder ->
    builder.allowBlockingCallsInside(
        "com.acme.LegacyService", "blockingMethod"));
```

**`Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` in tests**
- Adds operator-assembly stack frames to error traces
- Slow — enable in test or dev only, never in production

```java
@BeforeAll
static void enableDebug() {
    Hooks.onOperatorDebug();
}
```

**Common testing pitfalls — watch for:**
- **Forgetting `.verify()`** — `StepVerifier.create(flux).expectNext("a")` without `.verify()` does nothing; the test passes trivially
- **`.block()` in tests** — can deadlock on event-loop; use `StepVerifier`
- **No timeout on `verify()`** — default is infinite; slow tests hang CI; always `verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5))`
- **Cold vs hot publishers** — `TestPublisher` defaults to cold; `createCold` vs `createHot` if semantics matter
- **Virtual time** doesn't virtualize subscribers' real threads — only the scheduled clock
- **`@MockitoBean` returns null stubs** — reactive code throws; always `when(svc.find(...)).thenReturn(Mono.just(...))`
- **Reactive transactions** — `@Transactional` with R2DBC needs `R2dbcTransactionManager`; plain `@Transactional` doesn't help in reactive chains
- **Slow integration tests** — Testcontainers startup is seconds; reuse containers across tests with the singleton pattern
- **Port conflicts** — `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` prevents collisions in parallel runs
- **Context propagation** — MDC and tracing context need explicit `contextWrite` or Micrometer Context Propagation

**Performance tuning for tests:**
- Use test slices (`@WebFluxTest`, `@DataR2dbcTest`) instead of full `@SpringBootTest` when possible
- Reuse Testcontainers across test classes (singleton pattern)
- Parallelize at class level — JUnit 5 supports parallel execution
- Avoid `@DirtiesContext` unless necessary — it's expensive

**Coverage strategy / pyramid for a reactive service:**

| Layer | Count (approx) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Unit (`StepVerifier`) | 100 | Service logic, mappers, validation |
| Slice (`@WebFluxTest`) | 30 | Controller mapping, validation, error handling |
| Integration (`@SpringBootTest` + Testcontainers) | 10 | Full happy path through real DB |
| Contract (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) | 3 | Cross-service boundaries |

**The mental model:**
- Every reactive test needs a subscriber (`.verify()`, `.exchange()`)
- Every time-based test should use virtual time
- Every integration test should cleanly tear down async resources
- BlockHound on for all tests catches 90% of "reactive slowness" bugs
- Test the contract, not the implementation — `WebTestClient` over unit-mocked WebFlux internals

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`StepVerifier`** is the primary tool; always end with `.verify()` / `.verifyComplete()` / `.verify(Duration)`
- **`TestPublisher`** for controllable input sequences with explicit `next` / `error` / `complete`
- **`WebTestClient`** for WebFlux endpoints; slice mode (`@WebFluxTest`) or real server (`RANDOM_PORT`)
- **MockWebServer / WireMock** for mocking upstream `WebClient` calls
- **Testcontainers** for real Postgres / Mongo / Kafka integration
- **BlockHound** catches accidental blocking on event-loop threads — install for every reactive test class
- **`Hooks.onOperatorDebug()`** for readable stack traces in tests (slow; test-only)
- **Slice tests** are much faster than full context
- **Never `.block()` in tests** — always use `StepVerifier` or `WebTestClient`
- **Pyramid** — many unit, some slice, few integration, selective contract

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Reactive testing uses specialized tools because regular JUnit assertions don't wait for async signals.

**Core tools**
- `StepVerifier` — primary for `Mono` / `Flux`; chain expectations, end with `.verify()` / `.verifyComplete()` / `.verify(Duration)`
- `TestPublisher` — controllable input with explicit `next` / `error` / `complete`
- `WebTestClient` — endpoint testing; slice mode `@WebFluxTest` or real server `RANDOM_PORT`
- MockWebServer (okhttp) — fake upstream `WebClient` calls; WireMock alternative
- BlockHound — catches accidental blocking on non-blocking schedulers
- Testcontainers — real Postgres / Mongo / Kafka in Docker
- Spring Boot test slices — `@SpringBootTest`, `@DataR2dbcTest`, `@WebFluxTest`

**Test layers**
- Unit — pure Reactor chains with `StepVerifier`
- Slice — `@WebFluxTest` controller + mocked service
- Integration — `@SpringBootTest` + `WebTestClient` + Testcontainers

**StepVerifier patterns**
- Basic — `expectNextMatches`, `expectComplete`, `verify(Duration)`
- Counts — `expectNextCount(N).verifyComplete()`
- Errors — `expectError(Type.class)` or `expectErrorMatches(predicate)`
- Backpressure — `initialRequest(0)`, `thenRequest(N)`, `expectNextCount`, `thenCancel`
- Custom — `assertNext(block)`, `thenConsumeWhile(predicate)`

**WebTestClient patterns**
- Slice — `@WebFluxTest(Controller.class)` + `@MockitoBean Service`
- `client.get().uri().exchange().expectStatus().isOk().expectBody(Type).value(...)`
- Validation — `expectStatus().isBadRequest()` plus `ProblemDetail` body
- Streaming SSE — `returnResult(ParameterizedTypeReference)` plus `StepVerifier` on body
- Integration — `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` plus Testcontainers

**Mocking upstream**
- MockWebServer — enqueue responses, assert request count, body delay for timeouts
- WireMock — richer, heavier

**BlockHound and debug hooks**
- `BlockHound.install()` in `@BeforeAll`
- Whitelist legacy blocking with `allowBlockingCallsInside`
- `Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` for readable stack traces (slow; test-only)

**Common pitfalls**
- Forgetting `.verify()` — passes trivially
- `.block()` in tests — deadlock risk
- No timeout on `verify()` — tests hang CI
- `@MockitoBean` returns null — reactive throws; always `when().thenReturn(Mono.just(...))`
- Reactive transactions need `R2dbcTransactionManager`
- Slow integration tests — reuse Testcontainers as singletons
- Context propagation — MDC and tracing need explicit `contextWrite`

**Pyramid for a reactive service**
- 100 unit, 30 slice, 10 integration, 3 contract

**Strategic answer**
- `StepVerifier` for reactive chains; `.verify()` is mandatory
- Virtual time for delay-based operators (separate question)
- `WebTestClient` for endpoints; slice fast, real server for integration
- MockWebServer for upstream; Testcontainers for real DB / Kafka
- BlockHound catches accidental blocking
- Slice tests over full context where possible

questions.question: How do you test time-based reactive operators using StepVerifier virtual time?
questions.title: StepVerifier Virtual Time — Testing Delay-Based Operators
questions.direct_answer: Time-based operators like `interval`, `delayElements`, `delaySubscription`, and `timeout` would make tests slow if they ran in real time. **`StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(supplier)`** swaps Reactor's default scheduler for a `VirtualTimeScheduler` so emissions can be advanced instantly. You construct the `Mono` / `Flux` *inside* the supplier (so it picks up the virtual scheduler), then assert with `expectNoEvent(Duration)` to verify nothing fires before its time, `thenAwait(Duration)` to advance the clock, and `expectNext` to consume emissions. The test completes in milliseconds even when the pipeline simulates hours of behavior.

sections.title: Why Virtual Time Exists
sections.content:
Reactor has many time-based operators — `Flux.interval`, `Mono.delay`, `delayElements`, `delaySubscription`, `timeout`, `Retry.backoff`, `take(Duration)`. Tested in real time, they make CI painfully slow: a test of "emit every 100 ms for 10 seconds" actually takes 10 seconds.

**`StepVerifier.withVirtualTime`** replaces Reactor's default scheduler with a **`VirtualTimeScheduler`** — a controllable clock. Emissions scheduled for some future moment fire only when you advance the clock with `thenAwait(Duration)`. Tests of long-duration behavior complete in milliseconds.

**The contract**
- Build the `Mono` / `Flux` *inside* the supplier passed to `withVirtualTime`
- This ensures operators capture the virtual scheduler instead of the real one
- Use `expectNoEvent(Duration)` to verify nothing fires before its time
- Use `thenAwait(Duration)` to advance the clock
- Use `expectNext` / `expectComplete` / `expectError` as in normal `StepVerifier`

**What virtual time does NOT do**
- It does not virtualize subscriber threads or arbitrary concurrent code
- It does not affect non-Reactor schedulers (your own `ExecutorService`)
- It only controls the Reactor `Schedulers` clock — `Schedulers.parallel()`, `Schedulers.boundedElastic()`, etc.

sections.title: Basic Patterns
expectNoEvent vs thenAwait — the Subtle Difference
sections.content:
Both advance virtual time, but they assert different things.

**`expectNoEvent(Duration)`**
- Advances the clock by `Duration` *and* asserts that no event arrives during that window
- Use to verify timing — "nothing should fire before 100 ms"
- Fails if any signal arrives in the window

**`thenAwait(Duration)`**
- Advances the clock by `Duration` without asserting anything about events
- Use to fast-forward to the moment when you expect a signal
- Doesn't care what happens during the wait

**Example contrasting the two**

```java
// Asserts NO event before 100ms, then exactly the first emission
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() ->
        Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).take(3))
    .expectSubscription()
    .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofMillis(100))
    .expectNext(0L)
    .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(200))
    .expectNext(1L, 2L)
    .verifyComplete();
```

**Common mistake — building the publisher outside the supplier**

```java
// WRONG — Flux captured the real scheduler before withVirtualTime swapped it
Flux<Long> ticks = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).take(3);
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> ticks)
    .expectNext(0L, 1L, 2L)
    .verifyComplete();
```

The `Flux.interval` was created on the real scheduler — virtual time can't control it. The test will block waiting for real-time emissions. Always construct inside the supplier:

```java
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() ->
    Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).take(3))
```

sections.title: Configuring Custom Virtual Time
When Virtual Time Helps, When It Doesn't, and Pitfalls
sections.content:
**When virtual time helps:**
- Testing `interval`, `delayElements`, `delaySubscription`, `timeout`
- Testing `Retry.backoff` exhaustion without waiting minutes
- Testing scheduled emissions (cron-like flows)
- Testing rate-limiting / throttling operators
- Long-duration behavior compressed into a fast test

**When virtual time doesn't help:**
- Network or DB I/O — virtual time can't speed up real-world operations
- `CompletableFuture` or other non-Reactor async — virtual time only controls Reactor schedulers
- Tests where the actual elapsed wall-clock matters (rare)
- Multi-threaded race conditions — virtual time runs single-threaded internally

**Watch for — common pitfalls:**
- **Building the publisher outside the supplier** — the operator captures the real scheduler; the test hangs or fails
- **Using `expectNoEvent` when you mean `thenAwait`** — `expectNoEvent` will fail if any signal fires; pick the one that matches your intent
- **Mixing real and virtual schedulers** — if your code uses `Schedulers.boundedElastic()` for one branch and the chain has time-based ops, the virtual clock won't apply uniformly
- **Forgetting `expectSubscription`** — some chains emit immediately; including `expectSubscription` first avoids ordering surprises
- **Long `thenAwait` durations** — passing `Duration.ofDays(7)` is fine; just don't follow it with extra real-time operators
- **`VirtualTimeScheduler.reset()`** if you set it globally — leaking state across tests

**Testing `Retry.backoff` — a worked example**
- Three retries with 1-second base backoff and exponential growth
- Without virtual time the test runs for ~7 seconds
- With virtual time it runs instantly

```java
@Test
void retryBackoffWithJitter() {
    AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();

    StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() ->
            Mono.fromCallable(() -> {
                    int n = calls.incrementAndGet();
                    if (n < 4) throw new RuntimeException("fail " + n);
                    return "ok";
                })
                .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofSeconds(1))
                    .maxBackoff(Duration.ofSeconds(10))))
        .expectSubscription()
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
        .expectNext("ok")
        .verifyComplete();

    assertThat(calls.get()).isEqualTo(4);
}
```

**Strategic guidance:**
- Use virtual time for any test that includes `interval`, `delay`, `timeout`, or `Retry.backoff`
- Construct publishers inside the supplier — never outside
- Pick `expectNoEvent` vs `thenAwait` based on whether you want to assert silence or just advance
- For multi-second pipelines, prefer virtual time over `Awaitility` or sleep-based polling
- Combine with `TestPublisher` when you want to control both timing and input signals

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(supplier)`** swaps Reactor's scheduler for a controllable virtual clock
- **Build the publisher inside the supplier** — outside, it captures the real scheduler
- **`expectNoEvent(Duration)`** advances the clock and asserts no signal during the window
- **`thenAwait(Duration)`** advances the clock without asserting events
- **Use for `interval`, `delayElements`, `delaySubscription`, `timeout`, `Retry.backoff`**
- **Doesn't help** real network / DB I/O or non-Reactor async
- **Always start with `expectSubscription`** for predictable ordering
- **`VirtualTimeScheduler.set` / `.reset`** for global tests; use sparingly
- **Combine with `TestPublisher`** for full control of timing and input
- **Tests of long-duration behavior** complete in milliseconds

sections.content:
Time-based operators like `interval`, `delayElements`, `timeout`, and `Retry.backoff` would make tests slow in real time. `StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(supplier)` swaps Reactor's scheduler for a `VirtualTimeScheduler` so emissions advance instantly when you advance the clock.

- Use `expectNoEvent(Duration)` to verify nothing fires during a window
- Use `thenAwait(Duration)` to advance the clock without asserting
- Use `expectNext` / `expectComplete` / `expectError` as normal

**Basic patterns**
- `Flux.interval` — `expectNoEvent` for the first window, `expectNext`, then `thenAwait` for further emissions
- `Mono.delay` — `expectNoEvent` for the delay, then `expectNext`
- `delayElements` — `thenAwait` between each `expectNext`
- `timeout` — `thenAwait` past the timeout, then `expectError(TimeoutException.class)`
- `Retry.backoff` — `thenAwait` past the cumulative backoff, then assert success or error

**`expectNoEvent` vs `thenAwait` — the subtle difference**
- `expectNoEvent(Duration)` advances the clock and asserts no signal in that window
- `thenAwait(Duration)` advances the clock without asserting
- Pick the one that matches your intent

**Common mistake**
- Building the publisher outside the supplier — captures the real scheduler — test hangs
- Always build inside `() -> Flux.interval(...)`

**When virtual time helps**
- `interval`, `delayElements`, `delaySubscription`, `timeout`, `Retry.backoff`
- Long-duration pipelines compressed into milliseconds

**When it doesn't help**
- Real network / DB I/O — only Reactor schedulers are virtualized
- Non-Reactor async like `CompletableFuture`
- Multi-threaded race conditions — virtual time runs single-threaded

**Strategic answer**
- Use virtual time for any time-based operator test
- Construct publishers inside the supplier
- Pick `expectNoEvent` vs `thenAwait` based on whether you want to assert silence or just advance
- Combine with `TestPublisher` for full control of timing and input
- Tests of multi-minute behavior complete in milliseconds, keeping CI fast
